mcqs.question: Why does a `groupBy` operation require a shuffle even if the data is already spread across many partitions?
options: Because groupBy requires all data to first be sorted alphabetically by column name
Because the operation needs every value for a given key visible together on one task, but the key's values are initially scattered across partitions with no relation to that key
Because Spark cannot run groupBy without first writing the entire dataset to HDFS
Because groupBy can only execute on a single executor regardless of cluster size
mcqs.explanation: The data starts arranged by whatever partitioning happened to exist before (by file, by upstream logic), which has no relationship to the groupBy key — a shuffle is what physically brings each key's scattered values together onto one task. There's no alphabetical sort requirement, no HDFS write requirement, and groupBy runs across many executors in parallel, not on a single one.

mcqs.question: A Spark job is shuffle-bound and running slowly. Why might adding more executor cores provide little to no improvement?
options: Because more cores actively slow down disk I/O
Because a shuffle-bound job's cost is dominated by network transfer, disk I/O, and serialization, none of which shrink just because more CPU cores are available
Because Spark caps the number of cores any job can use to four
Because adding cores always requires restarting the entire cluster from scratch
mcqs.explanation: Shuffle cost is fundamentally about moving bytes across machines and disks, not about CPU-bound computation, so extra compute cores don't address the actual bottleneck. There's no fixed four-core cap, adding cores doesn't slow disk I/O, and it doesn't require a full cluster restart in normal operation.

mcqs.question: One customer_id has a million orders while every other customer has a few dozen. What effect does this have on a groupBy(customer_id) stage?
options: The stage automatically splits the skewed key's data across multiple tasks with no configuration needed
Nothing — Spark evenly distributes all keys' data across tasks regardless of key frequency
The task assigned that one key handles dramatically more data than every other task, and the stage isn't finished until that single task completes, no matter how fast the others ran
Spark throws an error and refuses to run the groupBy
mcqs.explanation: Because a shuffle sends all of one key's data to a single task, a wildly overrepresented key means one task carries a wildly disproportionate load, and the whole stage waits on that slowest task regardless of how quickly the rest finish. Spark does not auto-split a skewed key without specific techniques like salting or adaptive execution enabled, doesn't distribute evenly by default, and runs the job rather than erroring out.

mcqs.question: Why is salting a skewed key straightforward for a groupBy aggregation but trickier for a join?
options: Salting cannot be used with aggregations at all, only with joins
Joins do not support any form of key modification

A groupBy's sub-results can simply be summed back together after salting, while a join needs the salt applied consistently to both sides or matching rows end up on different sub-keys and never actually join
Salting only works when the cluster has fewer than 10 executors
mcqs.explanation: Aggregation is naturally recombinable — sum the salted sub-results and you get the true total — while a join needs both sides' matching rows to land on the same sub-key, which requires coordinated salting logic rather than a simple append. Salting is a real technique for both operation types, and executor count has no bearing on whether it works.

mcqs.question: A Spark job's UI shows 999 tasks in a stage completed within seconds, and one task still "running" after 20 minutes. What should you check first?
options: Restart the job immediately, since a stuck task means the cluster is unresponsive
Assume the cluster needs more executors and add them before investigating further

The per-task shuffle-read size and duration distribution for that stage, to check whether the one long-running task is handling disproportionately more data — a sign of skew rather than a cluster problem
Assume the job has a network outage and check cluster connectivity logs
mcqs.explanation: This exact pattern — one wildly slower task among many fast ones — is the classic skew signature, and checking the task's shuffle-read size confirms whether it's carrying disproportionate data. Restarting reproduces the identical result since the underlying data hasn't changed, adding executors doesn't help a single overloaded task, and this pattern isn't characteristic of a network outage, which would typically affect many tasks rather than isolate to one.

mcqs.question: A shuffle stage is configured with 50,000 tiny partitions on a modest cluster. What's the likely consequence?
options: The job will run faster because more partitions always means more parallelism
Scheduling and coordination overhead for tracking and dispatching tens of thousands of tiny tasks can exceed the actual work being done per task, slowing the job down
Spark will automatically merge them into a single partition before running
The job will fail immediately with a fixed partition-count error
mcqs.explanation: Over-partitioning trades useful parallelism for per-task overhead — at some point the driver's cost of tracking and dispatching enormous numbers of tiny tasks dominates over the tiny amount of real work each one does. More partitions doesn't unconditionally mean faster execution, Spark doesn't silently auto-merge excessive partitions by default, and there's no universal fixed error threshold that halts the job outright.
